content.text:
For a typical **common cold**, there’s no medicine that “cures” it—most colds improve on their own in about **7–10 days**. Medicines can help with symptoms. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/common-cold/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20351611?sf237848573=1&utm_source=openai))

**For adults, choose based on your symptoms:**

- **Fever, headache, sore throat, body aches:**  
  **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen**.  
  *Be careful not to double-dose acetaminophen*, since many cold/flu combo products contain it.

- **Stuffy nose/congestion:**  
  A **saline nasal spray**, or a short course of a decongestant such as **pseudoephedrine** or **oxymetazoline nasal spray**.  
  Avoid or ask a clinician first if you have **high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, prostate/urination problems**, or take certain medications.

- **Runny nose/sneezing:**  
  An antihistamine may help, especially at night. Some can cause drowsiness.

- **Cough:**  
  **Honey** can help calm cough in adults and children over 1 year old. OTC cough medicines may help some people, but results vary. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/acute-bronchitis/about/index.html?utm_source=openai))

- **General care:**  
  Rest, fluids, humidified air/steam, and throat lozenges can help.

**Avoid antibiotics** unless a clinician says you need them—colds are viral, and antibiotics don’t treat viruses. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**Important:** If this is for a **child**, especially under age 6, don’t use OTC cough/cold medicines without medical advice; they can cause serious side effects in young children. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/acute-bronchitis/about/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**Get medical advice urgently** if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, blue lips, dehydration, confusion, symptoms that worsen after improving, fever lasting more than a few days, or if you’re pregnant, elderly, immunocompromised, or have chronic lung/heart disease. Also consider testing for **COVID-19 or flu**, since antivirals may help some higher-risk people if started early. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))
